list.listitem: Cancer survivors should be strongly advised to stop using tobacco products, and provided assistance with tobacco cessation. A
Breast cancer survivors should receive annual mammography on remaining breast tissue. A

Colorectal cancer survivors should receive a multimodal, risk-based follow-up strategy which may include endoscopy, CT imaging, history and physical, and tumor antigen testing. PET scan is not recommended.B
Prostate cancer survivors who received definitive treatment for their cancer should have prostate specific antigen testing every 6-12 months for the first 5 years, then yearly. C

The apparently-healthy adult cancer survivor should generally receive the same screening and preventive interventions as would be recommended in a similar patient without a history of cancer, unless superseded by screening and preventive recommendations regarding the primary cancer. C
Guidelines for providers can be found on the American Cancer Society Cancer Survivorship Care Guidelines app found here.

This chapter will focus on the routine follow-up of adult patients with several common cancers. Elements of routine follow-up that will be considered here pertain to the periodic evaluation and testing for recurrence of those cancers after a patient has received primary treatment.
A cancer survivor is defined by the National Cancer Institute as an individual with cancer, from the time of cancer diagnosis through the balance of his or her life.
Breast cancer: 126/100,000 women newly diagnosed from 2013-2017.
Colorectal cancer: 37/100,000 adults newly diagnosed from 2013-2017.
Prostate cancer: 105/100,000 men newly diagnosed from 2013-2017.
There are 16.9 million cancer survivors in the US.
Of these, 22% are breast cancer survivors, 21% are prostate cancer survivors, and 9% are colorectal cancer survivors.
64% of all cancer survivors are age 65 or older.
18% of cancer survivors were diagnosed 20 or more years ago.
The direct costs of cancer were $183 billion in 2015.

The apparently-healthy adult cancer survivor should generally receive the same screening and preventive interventions as would be recommended in a similar patient without a history of cancer, unless superseded by screening and preventive recommendations regarding the primary cancer.
Cancer survivors should be strongly advised to stop using tobacco products, and provided assistance with tobacco cessation.

Cancer survivors who are functionally asplenic (risk factors include radiation in the area of the spleen, bone marrow transplant) should be vaccinated against pneumococcal pneumonia regardless of age.

Breast cancer survivors should avoid exogenous estrogens. They may also benefit from use of aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole) or selective estrogen receptor modulators (e.g., tamoxifen). These medications should be initiated only in consultation with physicians experienced in the primary treatment of breast cancer.
Since increased body weight is associated with higher mortality for all cancers, cancer survivors should try to maintain ideal body weight.
Excercise interventions in cancer survivors leads to improvements in anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue, physical functioning, and health-related quality of life.

In a systematic review of 210 studies of cancer patients, the prevalence of clinical depression in the first year after diagnosis was estimated at 15-20% and should be considered in follow-up of cancer patients beyond initial therapy.

Anticoagulant therapy for cancer-associated venous thromboembolsim (VTE) is generally continued for at least 3-6 months, and longer in some high-risk patients with active cancer. Data suggests that anticoagulation therapy for cancer-associated VTE can be stopped in patients cured of cancer, as long as there are no other persistent risk factors or indications for continuing VTE (recurrent VTE, thrompbophilia, atrial fibrilation, etc). The preferred agents according to 2021 ACCP guidelines are apixaban, edoxaban, and rivaroxaban.

A study comparing the risk of VTE at six months follow-up in 671 patients confirmed the non-inferiority of DOAC agents with the previously recommended low molecular weight heparin therapies. The VTE incidence was 6.1% versus 8.8%. Moreover, the patients on DOAC were more likely to adhere to their therapy suggesting increased benefit with time.

In cancer associated VTE a randomised trial in 1766 patients reducing the dose of apixaban after the first six months was as effective as maintaining full dose with a non-significant trend to reduction in bleeding complications.
summarizes the 5-year survival rates based on cancer site and stage at the time of diagnosis.

A UK based study in 2020 assessed whether recent cancer treatment (within previous 12 months) increased risk of death from COVID-19 compared to cancer patients treated more than 12 months before. There was no risk of increased mortality from COVID associated with recent treatment.

A meta-analysis has shown that contrary to conventional wisdom there is no survival benefit from clinical trial participation if high quality studies only are included in the analysis. This can be reassurance to patients who have been unable to participate in trials.
Periodic interval history and examination of the cancer survivor should be directed toward discovering early signs and symptoms of disease recurrence.

A cancer-relevant review of systems should attempt to elicit such general symptoms as unintended weight loss, bone pain, lymph node enlargement, as well as symptoms specific to the original disease site.

Physical examination should be directed toward discovering evidence of neoplastic disease such as subcutaneous or breast masses, lymphadenopathy, hepatic enlargement or nodularity, splenomegaly, and ascites.

With a growing number of cancer survivors there is a need to promote rehabilitation and return to work. A systematic review with 1652 patients concluded that multidisciplinary interventions using physical, psychological and vocational techniques could significantly improve rates of return to work.

In the elderly, further workup of suspected recurrent cancer is contingent on the patient's wishes to do so. This decision to pursue further workup must be individualized, with attention to the patient's pre-existing comorbidities and their anticipated impact on life expectancy and ability to tolerate additional cancer therapies.
Multicancer detection tests may eventually have a role in surveillance but that has not been sufficiently evaluated at this time.

For breast cancer survivors, annual mammography coupled with regular office visits is as effective as more intensive follow-up strategies. summarizes routine breast cancer follow-up from the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO). In short, they recommend history and physical every 3 to 6 months for 3 years, every 6 to 12 months for 2 more years, and annually thereafter, as well as annual mammography. Other tests are not recommended for asymptomatic patients without specific clinical findings.
Conider discontinuing annual mammograms in the patient with a life expectancy of less than 5 years or with advanced comorbidities

For colorectal cancer survivors, controversy exists regarding the optimal strategy for surveillance screening for recurrent disease. There has been a question whether more intensive surveillance strategies that include endoscopy and CT imaging result in improved mortality outcomes, but the particular combination of testing (endoscopy, abdominal imaging, blood tests), and optimal frequency of testing, was uncertain. Recent evidence suggests no overall benefit on cancer-specific or all-cause mortality from more intensive follow-up in patients with CRC.

The American Society of Clinical Oncology published guidelines in 2013 that recommend (): (1) CT of abdomen and chest annually for 3 years (add pelvic CT if rectal cancer); (2) history, physical, and CEA every 3 to 6 months for 5 years; (3) colonoscopy 1 year later, then every 5 years; and (4) PET scans are NOT recommended.

A clinical trial randomized 1202 patients with recent curative surgery for colorectal cancer to one of four approaches to surveillance: (1) CEA only, (2) CT only, (3) CEA and CT, and (4) no scheduled follow-up. The three follow-up groups all had higher likelihood of detecting a recurrence, but no strategy was better than another. All-cause mortality and disease-specific mortality were higher (non-significantly, 18.2% vs 15.9%) in the groups that had follow-up testing than in the group that did not.

For prostate cancer survivors, surveillance for disease recurrence for patients who received definitive therapy (either prostatectomy or radiation therapy) generally consists of PSA monitoring every 6-12 months for 5 year, then annually, (more frequent evaluation in men at high risk for recurrence and in candidates for salvage therapy). Digital rectal exams (DRE) should be considered on an annual basis especially in those with high recurrence risk and low pretreatment PSA, but little evidence exists supporting the benefit of routine DRE in identifying disease recurrence.
There is little benefit in performing routine DREs in patients after radical prostatectomy without any biochemical evidence of disease.

For men with prostate cancer who elect active surveillance rather than treatment (recommended for Gleason score <7) and who have an estimated life expectancy of at least 5 years, the ASCO recommends PSA testing every 3-6 months, DRE at least every year, and serial biopsies every 2-5 years. Active treatment should be considered if there is evidence of disease progression.

Society for Gynecologic Oncoogy guidelines (2017) recommend regular history and physical examinations with speculum and pelvic examination. The interval is every 6 months for the first 2 years for low risk patients, and every 3 months for high risk patients. After that, annually for low risk patients and every 6 months moving to annually for high risk patients. Cytology and imaging is recommended for suspected recurrence, but not for surveillance in asymptomatic patients.

Society for Gynecologic Oncoogy guidelines (2017) recommend history and physical examination every 3 to 4 months in years 0 through 2; every 4 to 6 months in years 2 to 3; every 6 months in years 3 to 5, and annually after that. CA-125 monitoring is optional, with CT or PET/CT recommended when recurrence is suspected.

"Choosing Wisely" recommendations regarding cancer surveillance: Don’t perform surveillance testing (biomarkers) or imaging (PET, CT, and radionuclide bone scans) for asymptomatic individuals who have been treated for breast cancer with curative intent.Don’t routinely recommend follow-up mammograms more often than annually for women who have had radiotherapy following breast conserving surgery.Don’t obtain routine blood work (e.g., CBC, liver function tests) other than a CEA level for surveillance for colorectal cancer.Don’t perform routine PET-CT in the initial staging of localized colon or rectal cancer or as part of routine surveillance for patients who have been curatively treated for colon or rectal cancer.
A systematic review concluded that yoga improves physical and psychological outcomes in cancer patients, including fatigue and quality of life.
Exercise can improve quality of life in cancer patients.

A Cochrane review specifically addressed interventions for fatigue and weight loss in patients on follow-up for cancer. It found a lack of robust evidence to support specific interventions and called for better studies with more standardised reporting.
Quitting smoking is essential.
Maintain a healthy weight.
Report unintended weight loss, unusual bleeding, and lumps/masses.

Recommended Surveillance for Breast, Colorectal, and Prostate Cancer Following Definitive Treatment.
feature.feature_body:
Breast Cancer Colorectal Cancer Prostate Cancer
History and physical exam Every 3-6 months for 3 years, then every 6-12 months for 2 years, then annually Every 3-6 months for 5 years, then annually Annual DRE, especially in those at high risk for recurrence or low pretreatment PSA
Imaging Annual mammography on any remaining breast tissue. Bone scan, CXR, ultrasound, CT, PET and MRI are not recommended for otherwise asymptoamtic patient with no specific findings. Chest and abdomen CTa annually for 3 years in patients at higher recurrence risk.b Rectal Cancer (only): consider pelvic CT if poor prognostic factorsc None recommended
Procedures None recommended Colon cancer: colonoscopy 1 year after surgery, then every 5 years thereafter if normal Rectal cancer: rectosigmoidoscopy every 6 months for 2-5 yearsd None recommended
Blood work None recommended (including CBC, chemistry panels, or tumor markers) in an otherwise asymptoamtic patient with no specific findings Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) every 3-6 months for 5 years PSA every 6-12 months fo 5 years, then yearlye
aIf patient could tolerate and would benefit from further intervention, e.g., surgery or systemic therapy. bHigher recurrence risk not strictly defined; usually means positive lymph nodes. cPoor prognostic factors includes no radiation therapy, but otherwise not strictly defined. dIf patient did not receive radiation therapy. eMay be considered more frequently in those at high risk (although high risk is not defined in this study).
